## Part 1: Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1**
- Pulpit: the better Greek reading says there was "again" a great crowd. It praises the crowd's eagerness: they stayed so long to hear Jesus that they ran out of food. (Pulpit)
- Utley: the setting is the mostly Gentile Decapolis area (compare Mark 7:31). (Utley)

**v. 2**
- Utley: the Greek word for "compassion" comes from the word for the inner organs, which Jews saw as the seat of feeling. "Three days" can mean parts of days, not three full days. (Utley)
- EW: the scene repeats the feeding of the 5,000. Jesus puts the problem in front of the disciples to see what they will do. (EW)

**v. 3**
- Ellicott and Pulpit: the Greek shows that "some have come from far" is Jesus speaking, not a comment by Mark. (Ellicott; Pulpit)
- Pulpit: Jesus waited until the people had nothing left, so they would feel both the blessing and the size of the miracle. (Pulpit)
- Utley: the "if" is about what could happen. Some were weak and might faint; not everyone was about to collapse. (Utley)

**v. 4**
- EW: Jesus hoped the disciples would remember what He had done before and trust Him for the present need. (EW)
- Gill: the disciples forgot the earlier miracle, even though this time there were fewer people and more food. (Gill)
- Utley: this was a test of their faith, and they failed it again. (Utley)
- PA cites Plummer, who reads the question as the disciples admitting they can't do it and leaving it to Jesus. It also cites McKenna, who sees more faith here than at the first feeding. (PA)
- Ellicott: the word for "desolate place" suggests loneliness. (Ellicott)

**v. 5**
- EW: this time the disciples had to give up their own food. (EW)
- Pulpit: the loaves were probably the group's own small supply. Jesus arranged different numbers each time so it would be clear these were two separate events. (Pulpit)

**v. 6**
- Ellicott and Pulpit: "sit" means reclining to eat. (Ellicott; Pulpit)
- Pulpit: the thanks was not asking for something uncertain; it showed Jesus' fellowship with the Father. The Greek tense shows the giving went on until everyone was fed. (Pulpit)
- EW: Jesus did what only He could do (the miracle), and left the disciples to do what they could do (hand out the food). (EW)

**v. 7**
- EW, quoting Ironside: the disciples may have held back the fish until they saw the bread multiply. (EW)
- Gill: Mark makes it look as if the fish were blessed separately, though Gill thinks bread and fish were probably eaten together. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/8-7.html)

**v. 8**
- Pulpit: there were seven baskets, as many as the loaves. The basket here (*spyris*) is a different word from the one in Mark 6 (*kophinos*), and was a larger, flexible basket like the one Paul was lowered in (Acts 9:25). Pulpit takes this as further proof the two miracles were separate events. (Pulpit)
- EW: they ended with more food than they started with, a sign of God giving out of abundance. (EW)

**v. 9**
- Gill: he follows Matthew in counting 4,000 men besides women and children, and pictures the healed people going home. (Gill)

**v. 10**
- Ellicott: Dalmanutha is named by no other writer, which shows Mark's independence from Matthew. (Ellicott)
- Pulpit places it on the western shore near Magdala. (Pulpit)

**v. 11**
- EW: the Pharisees wanted a dramatic sign in the sky, like Elijah's fire. Their "testing" echoes Satan's tempting of Jesus. (EW)
- Pulpit: they may have been hinting that Jesus' earthly miracles could come from Satan, so they asked for one from heaven. (Pulpit)

**v. 12**
- Gill: the sigh shows Jesus had a human soul that could feel grief. (Gill)
- Pulpit: the word for "sighed deeply" appears only here, and expresses grief mixed with indignation. "No sign shall be given" is a Hebrew oath form, a very strong refusal. (Pulpit)
- Ellicott: Mark leaves out "the sign of Jonah," which Matthew includes. (Ellicott)
- EW: Jesus' miracles were acts of mercy, not proofs aimed at people who had already hardened their hearts. (EW)

**v. 13**
- Constable: Jesus leaves the unbelievers, acting on the judgement He had just pronounced. From here on His ministry focuses more on the disciples. (Constable)

**v. 14**
- Ellicott: "one loaf" is a detail only Mark gives. (Ellicott)
- Pulpit: the conversation happened during a crossing of perhaps six hours. (Pulpit)

**v. 15**
- Pulpit: "leaven" means teaching. Matthew's "leaven of the Sadducees" is the same as Mark's "leaven of Herod." Pulpit quotes Jerome, who compares leaven to heresy spreading through the whole lump. (Pulpit)
- EW: Herod and the Pharisees both saw the kingdom as domineering power, political for one and religious for the other. (EW)
- Gill: lists possible links between Herod and the Sadducees. (Gill)
- MHC: the warning is against pride, hypocrisy and the traditions of the elders. (MHC)
- Utley: leaven stands for corruption. He suggests a possible Aramaic wordplay between "leaven" and "word." (Utley)
- Ellicott: the Greek tense means Jesus repeated the warning. (Ellicott)

**v. 16**
- Pulpit: the disciples may have been blaming each other. (Pulpit)
- MHC: distrust of God makes disciples quarrel among themselves. (MHC)
- EW: they could only think of bread for the stomach, not bread for the soul. (EW)

**v. 17**
- Ellicott: the question about hard hearts is found only in Mark, and is more vivid than Matthew's version. (Ellicott)
- Utley: the Greek form suggests a settled condition caused by an outside agent. (Utley)
- PA cites A. T. Robertson: Mark records six sharp questions that show Jesus' disappointment. (PA)

**v. 18**
- Gill: this means both their physical eyes and the eyes of their understanding. (Gill)
- MHC: failing to understand God's past kindness is the same as forgetting it, and that is what leaves us overwhelmed by worry now. (MHC)

**vv. 19–20**
- Pulpit and Utley: Jesus keeps the two words for "basket" distinct. The disciples remembered the facts but missed what they meant. (Pulpit; Utley)

**v. 21**
- Pulpit: the point is that Jesus was talking about teaching, not bread. Pulpit notes that Matthew says the disciples did then understand. (Pulpit)
- EW: Jesus' rebuke shows they could have done better. (EW)

**v. 22**
- Ellicott and Pulpit: only Mark records this miracle. The town is probably Bethsaida Julias, on the north-east shore. (Ellicott; Pulpit)
- Pulpit: the people who asked Jesus to "touch" the man were almost telling Him how to heal. (Pulpit)

**v. 23**
- Ellicott: Jesus suits His method to the man, as with the deaf man in Mark 7:33. The spitting also links Mark with John 9. (Ellicott)
- Pulpit: Jesus took the man aside for prayer and to avoid praise. (Pulpit)
- MHC: leading him out of town was a rebuke to unbelieving Bethsaida. (MHC)
- EW quotes Adam Clarke: the spittle may simply have separated eyelids stuck together. (EW)
- Constable: the man showed some faith by following Jesus out. (Constable)

**v. 24**
- Ellicott: the better manuscripts read "I see men, for I see them walking like trees." Ellicott reads it as a picture of a stage in spiritual growth. (Ellicott)
- Pulpit: the man saw blurred, oversized shapes. (Pulpit)
- Gill: likewise, the gospel at first lets in only a little light. (Gill)

**v. 25**
- EW: this is the only healing in the Gospels that happens in stages. It probably illustrates that the disciples' blindness would be healed gradually. (EW)
- Pulpit gives two reasons: to show Jesus is not tied to one method, and to match the healing to the man's growing faith. It quotes Bede on spiritual sight coming by degrees. (Pulpit)
- MHC agrees, but adds that Jesus did not always work by this rule. (MHC)
- NET note: the verb means "looked intently" or "stared with eyes wide open." (https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=mar+8:21-30)

**v. 26**
- Ellicott: Jesus prescribed quiet after the healing, and warns against hasty talk right after a first spiritual insight. (Ellicott)
- Pulpit: the man did not live in Bethsaida. Jesus avoided publicity because His miracles served His teaching. (Pulpit)
- Gill and MHC: Bethsaida's unbelief meant it would not see the healed man. (Gill; MHC)

**v. 27**
- Pulpit: Caesarea Philippi was a border region with many Gentiles, where Jesus could speak more freely about the Messiah. (Pulpit)
- Ellicott: the Greek tense suggests repeated, searching questions. (Ellicott)
- MHC: Jesus did not ask for His own information but so the disciples would think it through. (MHC)

**v. 28**
- Pulpit: explains why people guessed John the Baptist (similar age, and Herod's rumour) or Elijah (Malachi 4:5). (Pulpit)
- NET note: Elijah's coming meant the end time had arrived. (https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=mar+8:21-30)
- EW: John and Elijah were both national reformers, so people may have hoped for a political messiah. (EW)

**v. 29**
- EW: Jesus asks each disciple personally. Peter's confession was right but easy to misunderstand, because "Messiah" suggested a political king. (EW)
- NET note: "Christ" and "Messiah" both mean "anointed one." (https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?search=Mark+8:29&book=mark&chapter=8&verse=29)
- Constable: this confession is the centre of Mark's Gospel, and from here the story heads towards the cross. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/8-30.html)
- Constable also says that in Mark "Messiah" includes deity. (Constable)

**v. 30**
- Ellicott: if Peter stands behind Mark's Gospel, leaving out Jesus' promise to Peter (found in Matthew 16) shows Peter's humility. (Ellicott)
- MHC: the disciples would preach this later, but for now it had to stay secret. (MHC)

**v. 31**
- EW: the suffering was a "must" because of human sin and God's love (Isaiah 53). (EW)
- MHC: the disciples still expected an earthly kingdom soon. (MHC)
- Utley: "after three days" may echo Hosea 6:1–2 or Jonah. (Utley)

**v. 32**
- Ellicott: Jesus spoke "openly," without holding back, and that is what shocked the disciples. (Ellicott)
- Constable: the word for Peter's "rebuke" is a strong one. (Constable)
- MHC: Peter acted out of affection but took too much liberty. (MHC)

**v. 33**
- Ellicott: Jesus looked at all the disciples, not only Peter. (Ellicott)
- EW: Peter meant well but was used by Satan without knowing it, because his mind was on human things. Guzik links this to the "leaven" of v. 15. (EW)
- Utley: Peter was repeating Satan's wilderness temptation. "Get behind me" carries an Old Testament sense of rejection. (Utley)
- PA: the Greek tense shows a mindset that ruled Peter's thinking. (PA)

**v. 34**
- Ellicott: Jesus calls the whole crowd to hear this, which Luke's "he said to all" confirms. (Ellicott)
- EW: the cross meant only execution, a one-way walk down death row. Guzik quotes Wiersbe: denying self is not the same as occasional self-denial. (EW)
- PA: the desire to follow Jesus starts with the Spirit's work in the heart. (PA)

**v. 35**
- Ellicott: "and the gospel's" appears only in Mark and ties devotion to Jesus to His message. (Ellicott)
- Constable makes the same point. (Constable)
- EW: you only find life by losing it, the way a planted seed does. (EW)

**vv. 36–37**
- Ellicott: "soul" is better translated "life," and "forfeit" implies a penalty. (Ellicott)
- Utley: gaining the world was one of Satan's temptations, and "forfeit" means losing something you once had. (Utley)
- EW: Jesus Himself turned down the world (Luke 4). (EW)

**v. 38**
- Ellicott: the warning was especially aimed at disciples like Peter, who had just been "ashamed" of Jesus' words. (Ellicott)
- Barnes: the verse refers to the day of judgement. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/8-30.html)
- EW: siding with a despised, executed Messiah is costly, but leads to sharing His glory. (EW)

---

## Part 2: Where Protestant traditions differ

I found only one real disagreement, and it is not clearly between named denominations:

- **vv. 34–38, who the warnings are for.** Constable says they mean loss of reward for believers and loss of salvation for unbelievers. (Constable) The Precept Austin page reads v. 38 differently: being "ashamed" means a settled attitude of the heart, not a moment of cowardice. (PA)
- **Labels on StudyLight.** It tags Gill as "Baptist · Calvinism" (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/8-12.html) and *Contending for the Faith* as "Restoration Movement · Arminianism" (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/8-5.html). Neither entry I saw differs on doctrine.

I found no Methodist, Lutheran, Pentecostal or Anglican views on any verse.

---

## Part 3: Other views

Everything here comes second-hand from traditional writers. I read no Catholic, Orthodox, modern-scholarship or prosperity/word-of-faith sources.

- **vv. 1–10, two feedings or one?** EW and the Expositor's Bible report that some scholars think the 4,000 is a retelling of the 5,000. Both reject that view. (EW; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/mark-8.html) The Pulpit Homiletics adds that the 5,000 was mainly for Jews and the 4,000 mainly for Gentiles. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/mark/8.htm)
- **v. 8, the baskets as symbols.** The Expositor's Bible mentions a sceptical reading that makes the 12 baskets stand for the apostles and the 7 for the deacons. It rejects this. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/mark-8.html)
- **Older Catholic writers.** Pulpit draws on Cornelius a Lapide, a Catholic writer, for vv. 8, 25 and 27. (Pulpit)
